title: Boss: the 2 a.m. config fix
summary: Fix a broken config and a broken sudo rule on a server, with real keys and real tools.

steps.title: The pager went off
body: It is 2 a.m. A deploy changed two files on a server, and now nginx will not reload and the deploy user cannot restart the app.
You have an SSH session and nano. Three jobs, in rising order of risk:
1. Jump to the line `nginx -t` complains about and disable it.
2. Fix a wrong value everywhere in a file with one replace-all.
3. Fix a sudo rule **without locking everyone out of sudo**. A sudoers file with a syntax error can stop `sudo` working at all, so you check it with `visudo -c` before it goes live.

> **Why visudo:** `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy` opens the file in your `EDITOR` (nano, if you set it up) and refuses to save a file that does not parse. Editing sudoers with plain `nano` skips that safety net.

steps.title: Straight to line 5
prompt: In nano, jump straight to line 5 (Go To Line, `^_`) and comment the line out with `#`. On a real server you would then run `sudo nginx -t` again before `sudo systemctl reload nginx`.
steps.explain: Error messages give you a line number for a reason. `^_` (or starting nano with `nano +5 file`) takes you there in one step, even in a 2,000-line file. `nano -l` shows line numbers all the time.

steps.title: Replace all
prompt: The deploy pointed every upstream at `http:`. Switch every `http:` to `https:` with one **Replace** (`^\`, or `Esc R`), answering `A` for All.
steps.explain: Replace-all is safe here because the search text is specific. With a short or common search word, step through the matches with `Y` and `N` instead of `A`.

steps.title: Fix the sudo rule safely
prompt: The deploy user needs to run exactly one command as root: `/usr/bin/systemctl restart app`. A teammate wrote the rule in `~/deploy.sudoers`, but it has a syntax error.
1. Check the draft with `visudo -cf ~/deploy.sudoers` and read the error.
2. Fix the draft (this terminal is line based, so use `sed -i` or `vim -es` instead of nano).
3. Install it as `/etc/sudoers.d/deploy`, owned by root with mode `0440`.
4. Prove the whole sudo setup parses (`sudo visudo -c`) and that `sudo -l -U deploy` shows the rule.
If you break sudo itself, press **Reset scenario**: on a real server you would need the root password or a console to recover.

checks.name: /etc/sudoers.d/deploy is root-owned with mode 440
checks.fail: The rule is not installed as `/etc/sudoers.d/deploy` with owner root and mode 440 yet. `sudo install -o root -g root -m 0440 SRC DEST` does all three.

checks.name: the whole sudo setup parses
checks.fail: `visudo -c` reports an error. Fix the file it names.

checks.name: deploy may restart the app, without a password
checks.fail: `sudo -l -U deploy` does not list the rule. Is the tag written `NOPASSWD:` (with the colon)?

checks.name: deploy may run nothing else as root
checks.fail: The deploy user should have exactly one rule.

hints: `visudo -cf ~/deploy.sudoers` points at column 58 of line 2: right after `NOPASSWD`. Tags like `NOPASSWD` end with a colon.
`sudo install -o root -g root -m 0440 ~/deploy.sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/deploy`, then `sudo visudo -c` and `sudo -l -U deploy`.
steps.explain: Check first, install second. Mode 0440 matters: sudo ignores files in `/etc/sudoers.d` that others can write. On a real box, `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy` combines the edit and the check, and opens nano when `EDITOR=nano`.
